env.riskLow: Good conditions for outdoor foot care
env.riskModerate: Take care — conditions may affect foot care
env.rainWarning: Rainy conditions: Ensure feet are thoroughly dried after any outdoor exposure to prevent fungal infections.
env.airWarning: Air quality is poor: Limit outdoor exercise. For diabetic patients, poor air quality can impair circulation.
env.outdoorOK: Conditions are good. Take a short walk to improve circulation — beneficial for foot health.

iwgdf.label: IWGDF Risk Category
iwgdf.cat2: Category 2 — Two of LOPS / PAD / Deformity
iwgdf.catDesc0: No loss of protective sensation, no peripheral artery disease, and no foot deformity.
iwgdf.catDesc1: Loss of protective sensation OR peripheral artery disease is present (one of the two).
iwgdf.catDesc2: Two of the following are present: loss of protective sensation, peripheral artery disease, or foot deformity.
iwgdf.catDesc3: Loss of protective sensation or peripheral artery disease PLUS a previous ulcer, amputation, renal replacement therapy, or Charcot foot.
iwgdf.rulesDisclaimer: Based on IWGDF 2023 and NICE NG19 guidelines
iwgdf.careFacilitiesDesc: Hospitals and clinics with diabetic foot services in your area

neuropathy.lops: Loss of protective sensation — cannot feel the 10 g monofilament. Classify as IWGDF Category 1 and screen every 6–12 months.
neuropathy.symptoms: Burning, tingling, or numbness in the feet. Ask for nerve conduction studies if the symptoms are progressive or one-sided.
neuropathy.temperature: Cannot tell hot from cold water. Avoid hot foot soaks and test water temperature with an elbow or a thermometer.

skin.callus: Calluses, corns, or thickened nails. See a podiatrist for professional debridement — do not self-treat.
skin.fungal: Fungal infection between the toes or on the soles. Treat with an antifungal and dry thoroughly between the toes after washing.
skin.dry: Dry, cracked, or fissured skin. Moisturise daily (avoiding between the toes) and use a urea-based cream for cracks.

wound.active: An open wound, blister, or ulcer on the foot. See a foot-care team within 24 hours — do not delay.
wound.chronic: A wound that has not improved for more than 2 weeks. Urgent referral for advanced wound care and a vascular assessment.
wound.history: A previous foot ulcer, even if healed. This is IWGDF Category 3 — increased surveillance and custom footwear are required.

circulation.pulses: Absent or diminished foot pulses. Measure the ankle-brachial index (ABI); if ABI < 0.9, ask for a vascular assessment.
circulation.claudication: Leg or foot pain on walking, or pain at rest. Urgent vascular referral; antiplatelet and lipid management may be needed.
circulation.signs: Cold feet, colour change, or hair loss on the lower legs. Arrange a vascular assessment (toe-brachial index if ABI is unreliable).

selfcare.inspection: You are not inspecting your feet daily. Use a mirror to check the soles and set a daily reminder.
selfcare.footwear: Improper footwear or walking barefoot. Never walk barefoot, even indoors, and use properly fitted diabetic footwear.
selfcare.nails: Nail-cutting technique. Cut nails straight across and file the edges; see a podiatrist if you have neuropathy.

history.duration: Diabetes for more than 10 years. Increase foot-screening frequency — neuropathy and PAD risk rise with duration.
history.hba1c: HbA1c above 8% (64 mmol/mol). Intensify glucose management and ask about a referral to endocrinology.
history.amputation: A previous amputation. This is IWGDF Category 3, the highest risk — multidisciplinary care every 1–3 months, and take extra care of the other foot.

triage.title: Care Triage
triage.subtitle: Rule-based care navigation — not a diagnosis
triage.lockedNote: This care tier is determined by clinical rules and cannot be changed by AI-generated text.

actions.a1: Call 995 or go to the nearest Emergency Department now
actions.a2: Do not walk on the affected foot — keep it elevated
actions.a3: Do not apply creams, ointments, or home remedies
actions.a4: Do not soak the foot in water
actions.a5: Tell staff you have diabetes and bring your medication list

PRIMARY_CARE.facility: GP, polyclinic, or hospital diabetic foot clinic

actions.a1: Book an appointment with a GP or polyclinic within 24–48 hours
actions.a2: Keep the area clean and covered with a sterile dressing
actions.a3: Do not cut, pop, or self-treat the wound or blister
actions.a4: Wear protective, well-fitting footwear — do not walk barefoot
actions.a5: Photograph the area to show your doctor and track any change

SELF_CARE.facility: Self-care at home with close monitoring

actions.a1: Wash and dry your feet gently, especially between the toes
actions.a2: Apply moisturiser to the feet — but not between the toes
actions.a3: Offload pressure: avoid tight shoes and change position often
actions.a4: Inspect the area again in 24–48 hours
actions.a5: If redness spreads, pain worsens, or skin breaks, seek care promptly

ABSTAIN.timeframe: Before relying on this screening result

actions.a1: This tool cannot safely assess your situation from the information given
actions.a2: Please consult a healthcare professional (GP or polyclinic)
actions.a3: Do not delay care if your symptoms are getting worse

criteria.spreadingRedness: Redness spreading rapidly up the leg
criteria.alteredMentalState: Confusion, drowsiness, or systemic unwellness reported
criteria.shallowUlcer: Shallow ulcer or open wound without systemic signs
criteria.vulnerableRedness: Mild redness in a high-risk foot (prior ulcer/amputation or poor control)
criteria.pressureRedness: Mild pressure redness without skin breakdown
criteria.insufficientData: 2 or more red-flag questions were left unanswered, so a severe infection cannot be excluded

abstention.title: Unable to assess safely
abstention.contradictionDetail: Some of your answers conflict with each other. A healthcare professional can help clarify what is going on.
abstention.insufficientDetail: A severe foot infection is defined by a local infection plus a systemic response (SIRS), which needs at least 2 signs to confirm. Because 2 or more of those signs were left unanswered, we cannot rule it out. Please have your foot checked by a healthcare professional. If you feel unwell, seek care immediately.

home.welcomeSub: Your personal diabetic foot screening assistant
home.tip1: Inspect your feet daily for cuts, blisters, or color changes.
home.tip2: Moisturize your feet, but avoid getting lotion between your toes.
home.tip3: Wear well-fitting shoes and never walk barefoot.
home.dataSourcesDesc: Our screening logic is organized in 3 layers across 6 medical data and knowledge sources:
home.layer1Desc: Local disease prevalence and population context
home.layer2Desc: Authoritative clinical guidelines for triage and risk stratification
home.layer3Desc: Public datasets for risk profiling and safety/fairness validation
home.source1Desc: Core referral rules: limb-threatening red flags (gangrene, spreading infection, ischaemia), 24-hour referral, and annual foot screening
home.source2Desc: High-risk profiling: age, BMI, hypertension, stroke history linked to diabetes complications
home.source3Desc: International standard: from no sensory loss (Grade 0) to active ulcer or PAD (Grade 3)
home.source4Desc: Synthetic patient test data for end-to-end fairness testing across age, disease duration, and severity
home.source5Desc: Live weather and air quality data for environmental foot-care advisories; Singapore health statistics for population risk context
home.source6Desc: Critical infection thresholds: sepsis, systemic temperature/heart rate warning signs

assess.title: Foot Check
assess.subtitle: Comprehensive Assessment
assess.introDesc: This assessment covers 6 clinical categories based on IWGDF 2023 and NICE NG19 guidelines: red-flag screening, neuropathy, skin & nail, wound status, circulation, and medical history. Your profile provides additional self-care data. It takes about 2-3 minutes.
assess.firstTimeNote: First time using the app? Please fill in your profile first — it is used for your assessment result.
assess.resultsSubtitle: Your care recommendation is based on clinical rules. Discuss it with your healthcare provider.
assess.notDiagnosisNote: This is a preliminary risk indicator based on your self-reported symptoms. It is not a medical diagnosis. Please consult your healthcare provider for a proper evaluation.
assess.emergencyAction: Please seek medical attention within 24-48 hours.

questions.rf1: Do you have a fever (temperature above 38°C) or chills?
questions.rf2: Is redness spreading rapidly up your leg or beyond your foot?
questions.rf3: Is there any black, dead, or gangrenous tissue on your foot?
questions.rf4: Is there foul-smelling pus or discharge from your foot?
questions.rf5: Are you feeling confused, drowsy, or unusually unwell?
questions.w1: Do you have a foot wound or sore now, or have you had one before?
questions.w2: How long has this wound been there?
questions.w4: Compared with last week, is the wound getting better or worse?
questions.w5: Can you see bone, joint, or tendon inside the wound?
questions.sk1: Look at both feet. Tap everything you can see right now.
questions.n1: Can you feel your feet normally when touched?
questions.n2: Have you noticed any numbness, tingling, or burning sensation in your feet?
questions.n3: Can you feel a light touch (like a cotton swab) on your toes?
questions.n4: Do you get burning, tingling, or 'pins and needles' in your feet?
questions.n5: Do your feet feel numb, or like they are 'asleep'?
questions.n6: Have you had any falls, or felt unsteady on your feet, in the past year?
questions.n7: Has one foot become red, hot, or swollen, or changed shape recently?
questions.n8: Have your feet changed shape — for example hammer toes, bunions, or a high arch?
questions.n9: Can your feet tell hot from cold — for example, can you feel the water temperature in a bath?
questions.n10: Have you ever injured your foot — a blister, burn or cut — without feeling it until someone else noticed?
questions.s1: Have you noticed any changes in skin color on your feet?
questions.s2: Do you have calluses, corns, or areas of thickened skin on your feet?
questions.s6: Is the skin on your feet very dry or scaly?
questions.s7: Do you have itchy or white, cracked skin between your toes?
questions.s8: Are there areas of hard or thickened skin where your shoes rub?
questions.s9: Are your toenails thick, yellow, or curling into the skin?
questions.s10: Has the colour of your feet or toes changed (pale, blue, or dark)?
questions.s11: Is there redness, swelling, pain or pus where a toenail meets the skin?
questions.s12: Is there a dark or blood-coloured spot on your foot, or under a toenail?
questions.s13: Are there deep cracks in the skin of your heels that hurt or bleed?
questions.c1: Do your feet feel cold compared to the rest of your body?
questions.c2: Do cuts or sores on your legs or feet heal slowly?
questions.c3: Do you get cramping pain in your legs or calves when you walk?
questions.c4: Do you get pain in your feet or legs while resting, or at night?
questions.c5: Is the skin on your legs or feet shiny, tight, or losing hair?
questions.c6: Do your feet or ankles swell up during the day?
questions.c7: When your foot hangs down, does it turn red or dusky — and go pale when you raise it?
questions.c8: Compared with the other foot, is one foot noticeably colder, paler or more blue?
questions.g1: How have your blood sugar levels been over the past month?
questions.g2: Do you have any vision problems that make it hard to see your feet?
questions.h1: Has a doctor ever told you that you have nerve damage (neuropathy) or poor circulation in your feet?

options.w1a: No, and I have never had one
options.w1b: I had one in the past, but it has healed
options.w1c: Yes, I have a wound or sore now
options.sk1crack: Cracks or fissures in the skin
options.sk1blister: A new blister or fluid-filled bump
options.sk1red: Redness from pressure, with no break in the skin
options.n3a: Yes, I can feel it clearly
options.n9c: I cannot feel hot or cold
options.s8c: Yes, and they are painful or thick
options.s11c: Clearly red and swollen, or pus
options.c2c: Yes, often very slow to heal
options.c3b: Sometimes, but it eases when I rest
options.c3c: Yes, often, and it limits how far I walk

flags.redFlagFever: Fever or chills reported — possible systemic infection
flags.redFlagSpreading: Redness spreading rapidly — possible spreading infection
flags.activeWound: Active wound or sore detected on the foot
flags.chronicWound: Wound lasting more than 2 weeks — may indicate impaired healing
flags.historyUlcer: History of previous foot ulcer — high recurrence risk

assess.resultLowDesc: Your current foot risk is low. Continue your daily foot care routine, inspect your feet daily, and attend regular check-ups every 6-12 months.
assess.resultModerateDesc: Some areas of concern were identified. We recommend scheduling an appointment with your healthcare provider within the next 2 weeks for a thorough foot examination.
assess.resultHighDesc: Several concerning findings were detected. Please schedule an appointment with your healthcare provider as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours, or visit a walk-in clinic.
assess.resultUrgentDesc: Red flag findings detected that require urgent medical attention. Please contact your healthcare provider immediately or go to the nearest clinic/emergency department today.

reason.neuropathy: Because of your diabetes duration and control

recommendations.title: Care Recommendations
recommendations.subtitle: Personalized based on your assessment
recommendations.takeAssessment: Take an assessment to get personalized recommendations
recommendations.daily1: Inspect your feet every day, including between toes and the soles. Use a mirror if needed.
recommendations.daily2: Wash feet daily with lukewarm water and dry thoroughly, especially between toes.
recommendations.daily3: Apply moisturizer to feet but avoid the areas between toes.
recommendations.medNeuropathy: Your answers suggest possible nerve damage (neuropathy). Ask your doctor about monofilament testing and protective footwear.
recommendations.medSkin: Skin or nail changes were detected. Have your doctor or podiatrist examine these areas.
recommendations.medWound: A wound or sore was reported. Keep it clean and covered, and seek professional wound care.
recommendations.medCirculation: Possible poor circulation (PAD) detected. Ask your doctor about pulse checks and ankle-brachial index testing.
recommendations.medHistory: Your medical history increases your risk. Ensure regular foot screening by a healthcare professional every 3-6 months.
recommendations.medInsulin: Insulin use may indicate more advanced diabetes. Be extra vigilant with foot care and regular check-ups.
recommendations.medHbA1c: Your HbA1c is above 8%, indicating higher complication risk. Work with your doctor on blood sugar management.
recommendations.medSeeGP2weeks: Schedule a foot examination with your healthcare provider within the next 2 weeks.
recommendations.medSeeGP48h: See your healthcare provider within 48 hours, or visit an urgent care clinic.
recommendations.medRegular6to12: Schedule a professional foot examination every 6-12 months.
recommendations.medReportChanges: Report any new wounds, color changes, or symptoms to your doctor promptly.
recommendations.lsSelfCare: Your self-care routine needs improvement. Set a daily reminder to inspect your feet.
recommendations.lsSmoking: Quitting smoking significantly reduces foot complications. Ask your doctor about smoking cessation programs.
recommendations.lifestyle1: Wear comfortable, well-fitting shoes at all times. Never walk barefoot, even indoors.
recommendations.lifestyle2: Trim toenails straight across and file sharp edges. Avoid cutting too short. Consider a podiatrist for nail care.
recommendations.lifestyle3: Stay active with gentle exercises like walking to improve circulation. Aim for 30 minutes daily.
recommendations.noAssessment: Take an assessment to receive personalized care recommendations.
recommendations.learnMoreText: These recommendations are generated based on your self-reported assessment answers and profile, following IWGDF 2023 and NICE NG19 clinical guidelines. They are not personalized medical advice. Always follow your healthcare provider's specific instructions.

followup.title: Follow-up
followup.subtitle: Track your progress
followup.noHistory: No assessment history yet. Complete your first assessment to start tracking.
followup.checkinQuestion: Did you inspect your feet today?
followup.escalated: Your care tier has escalated compared with your last check. Seek care sooner and review the recommendations.
followup.stable: Your care tier is stable or improved compared with your last check. Keep up your self-care routine.
followup.noPrevious: Complete another check to compare it with your previous result.

recheck.title: Dynamic Re-check
recheck.subtitle: Update how your foot looks or feels now. The system compares it with your last check and tells you if you need a higher level of care.
recheck.noAssessment: You have not completed a foot check yet. Please take an assessment first, then use the dynamic re-check.
recheck.updatePrompt: Update your key foot status below:
recheck.notePlaceholder: e.g. Yesterday's red mark is bigger today and has some pus
recheck.disclaimer: For care navigation only; not a diagnosis. If symptoms worsen, seek care immediately.
recheck.escalatedReason: Your situation is more serious than last time. Your care tier has been raised. Follow the guidance below and seek care promptly.
recheck.stableDesc: Compared with your last check, your care tier has not gone up. Continue following the current guidance and re-check on time.
recheck.abstainDesc: Based on your update, the system cannot safely assess your situation. Please consult a healthcare professional.
